claims.text: Conventional spark-plasma-sintered or copper-infiltrated W–Cu composites typically exhibit interfacial voids.
Conventional spark-plasma-sintered or copper-infiltrated W–Cu composites typically exhibit phase separation or microstructural inhomogeneity.
Vapor deposition before copper infiltration can produce a nanoscale Ni interlayer on tungsten surfaces.
A nanoscale Ni interlayer promotes wettability between tungsten and copper.
A nanoscale Ni interlayer promotes chemical bonding between tungsten and copper.
The Ni interlayer lowers the interfacial energy between tungsten and copper.
Lower W–Cu interfacial energy improves copper wetting of tungsten.
Improved wetting reduces capillary defects during copper infiltration.
Improved interfacial bonding reduces void formation in the W–Cu composite.
Improved interfacial bonding reduces phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
Reduced void formation and phase separation produce a more homogeneous W–Cu microstructure.
A more homogeneous interfacial microstructure better maintains thermal conductivity under irradiation.
A more homogeneous interfacial microstructure better maintains mechanical integrity under irradiation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have a lower void fraction than otherwise identically processed composites without an interlayer.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have improved interfacial contact relative to composites without an interlayer.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher effective thermal conductivity than composites without an interlayer.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have greater mechanical durability during simulated fusion-reactor thermal cycling and irradiation than composites without an interlayer.
Oxidation of the constituent surfaces can be limited by processing in an inert atmosphere or high vacuum.
Unwanted interfacial reactions or Ni-interlayer degradation could negate the expected performance improvement.
Intermetallic formation involving the Ni interlayer could cause embrittlement.
